findings.finding: The contingency path's bounded-exposure rationale for raising http_put_response_hop_limit to 2 rests on a topology invariant — 'only first-party rebar containers share the default bridge' — that is not stated as a maintaining condition in the required ADR entry. If a future operator adds any container (e.g. a monitoring agent, a third-party sidecar, or a test image) to the same host without knowing this invariant applies, the safety boundary silently expands to include that untrusted container, invalidating the recorded exception's bounding argument.
findings.location: Approach section (contingency) + AC6: 'the exception with its bounded-exposure rationale is recorded in ADR 0046'
scenarios: A future story adds a monitoring sidecar (e.g. a Datadog or Prometheus agent container) to docker-compose.yml without realising the hop-limit=2 setting means it can now reach IMDS and acquire instance credentials.

findings.finding: The plan grants `bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream` but the testing section exclusively verifies the `Converse` API operation. Per AWS documentation, `ConverseStream` (the streaming Converse variant) uses the IAM action `bedrock:InvokeModel`, not `bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream`. The `InvokeModelWithResponseStream` action gates the older, non-Converse streaming API (`bedrock-runtime InvokeModelWithResponseStream`). If the review-bot will use `ConverseStream` for streaming, the correct IAM action is already covered; if it will use `InvokeModelWithResponseStream` (the old API), the AC never verifies that path. The plan does not state which streaming path the bot will actually use.

findings.finding: The iptables containment mechanism presupposes per-container network isolation that the current docker-compose.yml does not provide. The compose file defines no named Docker networks, so all three containers (gerrit, review-bot, opcert) share a single default bridge. There is no distinct network interface the plan can allow-list for review-bot and block for others; and blocking IMDS on the shared bridge would also break the opcert container's existing instance-role credential access (it fetches SSM params via boto3). The plan's security claim — 'blocks 169.254.169.254 from every container network on the box except the review-bot's' — is mechanically unsound against the actual compose topology unless the compose file is also changed to give each container (or at least review-bot) its own Docker network with a distinct bridge interface.

findings.finding: The plan's core security contract — 'blocks 169.254.169.254 from every container network on the box except the review-bot's' — assumes per-container or per-network differentiation that the existing docker-compose.yml does not provide. The compose file defines no named Docker networks; all three containers (gerrit, review-bot, opcert) share the default bridge. With a single shared bridge, an iptables DROP rule targeting '169.254.169.254 for non-bot networks' has no network interface or subnet to bind to, making the containment control unimplementable as described. The plan's Scope section does not list docker-compose.yml as a file to modify, and does not describe how named networks will be introduced. Without this, the accepted-limitation entry in ADR 0046 would document a control that does not actually exist, leaving every container on the host (including gerrit and opcert) able to reach the node role after the hop-limit is raised.
